rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and turns missing evidence into proof gates, not decoration. Its "Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part of going global, not the card itself" is a real infrastructure angle with the right proof asks. B has useful material, especially "When Your Company Goes Global but Your Corporate Card Doesn't," but "Brex's 50-Country Push Is Also a $12.3 Billion Bet" drags an old valuation into a launch story and starts spending evidence it does not have.
gaps_in_A: A misses a clean buyer-pain angle. It says "the buyer is now an enterprise treasury/finance org" but never turns that into a standalone CFO/controller workflow story.
"Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part" is plausible, but "hard part" is still an assertion from outside the update. Keep it, but make the proof gate non-negotiable.

A correctly refuses "Brex's international launch validates its $12.3B valuation," but it does not salvage the narrower, legitimate question: whether global expansion changes Brex's late-stage financial story.
gaps_in_B: "Brex's 50-Country Push Is Also a $12.3 Billion Bet" is the weak boardroom-think angle. The update gives an old valuation and undisclosed profitability, not a fresh financing or revenue story.
"Traditional Issuers Have Long Owned" and "historically been the incumbent advantage" are plausible market context, but they are not in the supplied facts. A reporter will ask, "Says who?"
"Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story" overstates category history from one company update. That is thesis cosplay unless backed by outside market evidence.
"local reimbursement delays, FX friction, and employee complaints about out-of-pocket costs" may be true, but the update does not say it. Treat it as a customer-interview hypothesis, not copy.
